chunks: I heard him saying: 'Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said: Upon the Imams are obligations that are not upon their followers, and upon our Shia are obligations that are not upon us. God Mighty and Majestic commanded them to ask us, saying: "So ask the People of the Reminder if you do not know" [16:43]. Thus He commanded them to ask us, and it is not incumbent upon us to answer — if we wish, we answer, and if we wish, we refrain.

key_terms.أَهْلَ الذِّكْرِ: People of the Reminder — in Shia exegesis, refers to the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, not the Jewish scholars as some Sunni exegetes hold
key_terms.الْجَوَابُ: The answer/response — the Imam's response to questions is a divine prerogative, not a compulsion
key_terms.الْفَرْضُ: Obligation, divine duty — distinct between levels of the religious hierarchy

ai.seo_question: What obligations are unique to the Imams according to Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Ridha (AS) transmits a teaching from Imam Zayn al-Abidin (AS) stating that the Imams bear unique obligations not shared by their followers, and the followers bear obligations not shared by the Imams. God has mandated that people ask the Imams (the Ahl al-Dhikr) when ignorant, citing Quran 16:43, yet the Imams are not obligated to answer every question — they may exercise discretion in responding. This establishes a hierarchical structure of religious duty unique to the imamate, distinguishing the burden of divine leadership from ordinary discipleship. The audience — early Shia scholars around al-Kulayni's time (early 4th century AH) — would have understood this as a defense of the Imam's divine prerogative in dispensing knowledge.
